procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Additional Sessions Judge Saran
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 30, 1968 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 539 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Patna High Court maintained the conviction and sentence of the appellant (Gudar Dusadh), while some modification was made as regards the sentence awarded to the other five convicted accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Gudar Dusadh appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The leave was confined only to the question of whether the offense committed by the appellant was murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence committed by the appellant was murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

facts: The appellant and his companions were lying in wait to attack the deceased, Ramlal.
The assault was premeditated, and there was no prior altercation or exchange of abuses.
The appellant struck the deceased a single, deliberate blow on the head with a lathi (a type of stick).
The blow caused a 3-inch long fracture of the left parietal bone.
The deceased fell down and died instantaneously.
Medical evidence confirmed that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
law: The Court applied clause "3rdly" of Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code.

According to this clause, culpable homicide is murder if the act is done with the intention of causing a bodily injury, and that specific bodily injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
application: The Court broke down the application of clause "3rdly" into two parts.

First, it determined that the appellant had the intention to cause the specific injury that was inflicted. The assault was premeditated, the blow was aimed at the head, and it was not accidental. The fact that only one blow was struck did not mitigate the offense.
Second, relying on the medical evidence, the Court found that the injury inflicted (the fractured skull) was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

The Court distinguished a case cited by the appellant (Chamru Budhwa v. State of Madhya Pradesh) by noting that the present case involved a premeditated attack, not a sudden fight in the heat of passion.
reasoning.conclusion: Since both conditions of clause "3rdly" of Section 300 were met—the appellant intended to cause the specific head injury, and that injury was sufficient to cause death—the Court concluded that the offense was murder. It rejected the appellant's argument to reduce the charge to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and upheld the conviction under Section 302.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offence committed by the appellant was murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, relying on the precedent set in Chamru Budhwa v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
He contended that the fatal injury, caused by a single blow, was not inflicted with the intention of causing death or a bodily injury likely to cause death.

It was implied that the case should be covered by exception 4 to section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, as the crime was committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, similar to the facts in the cited case.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the offence was murder, falling squarely under clause "3rdly" of section 300 of the Indian Penal Code.
The assault was premeditated, and the blow to the deceased's head was deliberate and not accidental.
The appellant's act of aiming a lathi blow at the head showed a clear intention to cause that specific injury.
The medical evidence established that the injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The fact that only one blow was delivered does not mitigate the offence from murder to culpable homicide.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If an accused deliberately inflicts a bodily injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and death results, the offense is murder under clause '3rdly' of Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code. The fact that only one blow was delivered does not, by itself, mitigate the offense to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
obiter: The observation in Chamru Budhwa v. State of M.P. that a fatal injury from one blow was not caused with the intention of causing death or a likely fatal injury, was made in the specific context of that case's facts, which involved a sudden fight in the heat of passion falling under Exception 4 to Section 300.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's act constituted murder under clause "3rdly" of section 300 of the Indian Penal Code. The assault was premeditated, and the blow to the deceased's head was deliberate, not accidental. The fact that the appellant aimed a lathi blow at the head demonstrates an intention to cause that specific injury. As the medical evidence established that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, both parts of the legal test for murder under clause "3rdly" were satisfied.
legal_tests_applied: Clause "3rdly" consists of two parts. Under the first part, it has to be shown that there was an intention on the part of the accused to inflict the particular injury which was found on the body of the deceased. The second part requires that the bodily injury intended to be inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. So far as the first part is con-cerned, the court has'to see whether the injury which was fcillnd :m the deceased was the one intended by the accused or whether it was accidental without his having intended to cause that bodily injury. Once it is found that the injury was not accidental and that the accused intended to cause the injury which was actually inflicted and found on .the body of the; deceased, the first part shall be satisfied. The court would then go into the second part of the clause and find in the light of medical evidence as to whether the bodily injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. If the court finds that the requirements of both the parts have been satisfied, the case shall be held to be covered by clause "3rdly" unless it falls within one of the excep-tions.
why_appellant_lost: The precedent cited by the appellant, Chamru Budhwa v. State of Madhya Pradesh, was distinguished as it involved a crime committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, falling under exception 4 to section 300, which was not the situation in the present case.
The court rejected the proposition that a single deliberate blow to the head with a lathi, causing an injury sufficient to cause death, would not fall under clause "3rdly" of section 300.

The argument that the single blow mitigated the offence was dismissed, with the court stating: "The fact that the accused gave only one blow would not mitigate the offence and make l:iim guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder".
why_respondent_won: The court found that the first part of the test under clause "3rdly" was met because the injury was not accidental. The court reasoned: "The fact that the appellant aimed a blow on the head of Ramlal with the lathi would go to show that it was the intention of the appellant to cause the precise injury which was found on the head of the deceased."

The court found that the second part of the test was satisfied based on the medical evidence. The court stated: "The evidence of Dr. R. S. Singh who performed post mortem examination shows that the above injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death and actually resulted in the death of the deceased."

The court concluded that since both parts of the clause were satisfied, the case fell squarely within the ambit of murder: "As the injury on the head was deliberate and not acctdental and as the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the case against the appellant would fall squarely within the ambit of clause '3rdly' of section 300 Indian Penal Code."
